newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares seen cautious on new trade policy.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares seen cautious on new trade policy.

text.p: Indian stocks could make selective gains as the new fiscal year gets under way in the coming week, but the introduction of a freer trade policy could also hit some domestic firms, brokers said.
"A slight upward movement is all that I expect," said Kayu Mehta, chief investment officer at Tata Investment Corporation. "It can gather momentum only by May."
On Monday, the market is likely to be pushed by big local funds who will be looking for stronger closing prices to tidy their books, analysts said.

But lower tariffs and easier import norms would make buyers circumspect and choosy. The new five-year policy beginning from April 1 will tear down trade barriers as set out by the World Trade Organisation, they said.
"The market has already started to discount the trade policy," Mehta said. "Whatever commodity is overpriced will have a problem. It will not be a painless transition."
The 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange index ended 66.67 points, or 1.79 percent, lower at 3,663.53 last Friday from a week earlier.
"You could see a shake-out," said Alok Churiwala at brokerage Gaurishanker Churiwala. "The inefficient companies will close down. It will make Indian firms leaner and meaner."
He said freer consumer goods imports would hit makers of electronics, televisions, refrigerators and washing machines.
But shares of export-oriented companies could rise as they were likely to be given incentives, analysts said. Farm and marine exports were also likely to benefit.

A relaxation in imports should also have a beneficial impact on inflation as it would soak up robust dollar inflows and relieve the central bank from market interventions to keep the rupee from appreciating, analysts said.

Foreign exchange reserves stood at $25.14 billion on March 21, according to latest official data, against $24.66 billion a week earlier. Annual inflation as measured by the wholesale price index was inching up to eight percent.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has been pumping rupee funds into the banking system to buy dollars, but the excess cash has been helping build inflationary pressures.
Mehta said freer imports would help bring prices down.
The market's focus would also shift to the RBI's credit policy for the first half of fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) on April 15, dealers said.

The central bank is likely to trigger a cut in lending rates because of easier liquidity conditions. The prime rate of domestic banks should come down by 0.50 percentage point from their current 14.5 percent, the analysts said.
Agrochemicals and pesticides shares are expected to perform well thanks to strong farm output and good monsoon rains last year, Mehta said.
Shares of cotton yarn firms also looked good because they could compete globally, while some paint stocks offered attractive valuations, he said.
